Olfactory means relating to the sense of smell. Whenever you see this word attached to something, it is telling you that the thing it describes has to do with smelling.

Think of it as a family of similar adjectives: "visual" relates to sight, "auditory" relates to hearing, "tactile" relates to touch, and olfactory relates to smell. It belongs to that same pattern — one precise adjective for each sense.
What Kinds of Things Can Be "Olfactory"?

Since "olfactory" is an adjective, it always sits beside a noun and tells you what kind of thing it is. It can describe a remarkably wide range of things, all sharing one thread: they involve smell in some way.

Body parts and biological structures. The body has an entire network dedicated to detecting smells. The olfactory nerve is the nerve that carries smell signals from your nose to your brain. The olfactory bulb is a small structure at the front of your brain that first processes those signals. The olfactory receptors are the tiny cells inside your nose that actually detect odor molecules floating in the air. The olfactory system refers to all of these parts working together as one unit. In every case, the word "olfactory" is simply a precise way of saying "the smell-related part."

Sensations and experiences. You might read about an olfactory sensation — meaning the feeling or perception of a smell — or an olfactory experience, which refers to the overall encounter with smells in a given moment or place. Walking into a bakery and being hit by the warm scent of bread is an olfactory experience.

Memory. One of the most fascinating uses of this word is olfactory memory — a memory that is triggered by a smell. Scientists have found that smells connect to memory more powerfully than any other sense. When the scent of something — a perfume, a food, a place — instantly transports you back to a moment in your past, that is your olfactory memory at work.

Signals and cues. In biology and animal behavior, you will often read about olfactory cues or olfactory signals — smells that carry information. Animals use these constantly. A dog sniffing another dog is reading olfactory signals. Flowers producing sweet scents to attract bees are sending olfactory cues.

Looking at the word in real sentences is one of the fastest ways to make it stick.

  • The doctor examined the patient's olfactory nerve after he reported losing his sense of smell.
  • Perfumers train their olfactory abilities for years to distinguish hundreds of scents.
  • The old wooden cabin triggered a powerful olfactory memory — it smelled exactly like her grandmother's house.
  • Many animals rely on olfactory cues to find food, detect predators, and identify mates.
  • The olfactory system begins working the moment an odor molecule enters your nose.

In each of these, you could replace "olfactory" with the phrase "related to smell" and the sentence would still make perfect sense. That substitution test is a reliable way to check whether you have understood the word correctly.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

"Olfactory" is a formal, precise adjective. You will most commonly see it in three places:

In science and medicine, it is standard vocabulary. Doctors, biologists, neuroscientists, and researchers use it constantly because it is specific and leaves no room for ambiguity.

In literature and descriptive writing, authors who want to write with sophistication sometimes use "olfactory" to elevate their prose — for example, writing about "an olfactory assault" rather than simply "a terrible smell."

In everyday conversation, people almost never say "olfactory." They just say "smell," "scent," or "nose." If someone at a dinner table said "that was an olfactory delight," it would sound overly formal. The word belongs to academic and professional contexts, not casual chat.

Here is the single most important thing to hold onto: olfactory never means smell itself — it means related to smell. A rose has a smell. The nerve that carries that smell to your brain is the olfactory nerve. The memory the smell triggers is an olfactory memory. The receptor cells that detect it are olfactory receptors. The word always points one step to the side — to the mechanism, the system, the experience, or the biology surrounding smell, rather than to the smell itself.

Once you grasp that, the word will never confuse you, no matter which noun it is placed beside.
